title: Design an Online Shopping Cart — User, Product, Cart, CartItem, Coupon/Discount, checkout flow, inventory check, payment integration.

s1_definition.profdef: An online shopping cart design models a User holding a Cart of CartItems, each referencing a Product and quantity, with discount application, inventory validation at checkout, and payment integration. Core abstractions are User, Product, Cart, CartItem, a discount strategy, and a checkout service.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the shopping cart as a payment basket at National Bank of India's online store. Rajesh adds items to his basket, each with a quantity and price. When he checks out, the system totals the basket, applies any coupon he has, confirms the items are actually in stock, charges his account, and reduces inventory. The cart is just a running tally until checkout turns it into a real transaction.
s1_definition.oneliner: A shopping cart totals items, applies discounts, validates inventory at checkout, and charges payment atomically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An online shopping cart design models a User holding a Cart of CartItems, each referencing a Product and quantity, with discount application, inventory validation at checkout, and payment integration. Core abstractions are User, Product, Cart, CartItem, a discount strategy, and a checkout service.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the shopping cart as a payment basket at National Bank of India's online store. Rajesh adds items to his basket, each with a quantity and price. When he checks out, the system totals the basket, applies any coupon he has, confirms the items are actually in stock, charges his account, and reduces inventory. The cart is just a running tally until checkout turns it into a real transaction.

**One line to remember:** A shopping cart totals items, applies discounts, validates inventory at checkout, and charges payment atomically.

sections.s2_technical:
A `Cart` holds a list of `CartItem`, each a `Product` with a quantity. The subtotal is the sum of price times quantity across items. A `DiscountStrategy` applies coupons — flat, percentage, or buy-one-get-one — so adding a promotion type is a new class rather than an edit, which is the Strategy pattern.

Checkout is the critical flow. It validates inventory for every item, applies discounts to compute the final total, charges payment, and only then decrements stock. These steps must be atomic: if payment fails, no stock is deducted, and if stock is insufficient, no payment is taken.

```java
BigDecimal total = checkout.process(cart, coupon);
```

The senior nuance is the race between adding to cart and checking out: stock can sell out between the two, so the authoritative inventory check happens at checkout under a lock or an atomic decrement, not when the item is added. I also keep money in BigDecimal and separate the cart's display subtotal from the authoritative checkout total.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh adds two items to his cart and applies a ten-percent coupon. The system must total correctly and apply the discount. This is exactly the cart totalling and discount-strategy logic.

Problem 2 — At checkout, one item must still be in stock, and payment must succeed before stock is deducted, with nothing half-done. This is exactly the atomic checkout flow.

The code defines `Product`, `CartItem`, `Cart`, a `DiscountStrategy`, and a `CheckoutService`, with a demo where Rajesh checks out with a coupon.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a gold coin priced 6000 with 10 in stock, Rajesh adds 2 to his cart and checks out with a ten-percent coupon.

Step 1: `cart.add(coin, 2)` creates a cart item; `subtotal` computes 6000 times 2 equals 12000. Step 2: `process` first checks inventory, confirming 10 in stock covers the 2 requested. Step 3: the percentage discount reduces 12000 by ten percent to 10800, the final charge. Step 4: payment is logged, then stock is deducted by 2, leaving 8. No stock was touched before the inventory and payment steps passed.

```
Oct 31 22:18 INFO CART: Charging 10800.00 for SAV2001
Oct 31 22:18 INFO CART: Paid total=10800.00, stock left=8
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rajesh: cart.add(Gold Coin ×2)
     │ subtotal = 6000 × 2 = 12000
     ▼
  CheckoutService.process(cart, 10% coupon)
     │ inventory check: stock 10 ≥ 2 ✓
     │ discount: 12000 → 10800
     │ payment: charge 10800
     │ deduct stock: 10 → 8
     ▼
  order confirmed, total=10800
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I design an online shopping cart, I model a User holding a Cart of cart items, where each item references a Product and a quantity, and the cart computes a running subtotal by summing price times quantity. The cart itself is just a tally; the real work and the real risk live in the checkout flow.

Discounts are the first place I apply good design. I pull coupon logic into a discount-strategy interface with implementations for flat, percentage, and buy-one-get-one promotions, so marketing can launch a new promotion as a new class rather than forcing a change to the checkout code, which is the Strategy pattern and the Open/Closed principle together.

Checkout is the critical, must-be-atomic flow. It validates inventory for every item, applies discounts to compute the authoritative final total, charges payment, and only then decrements stock. The ordering matters: if payment fails, no stock is deducted, and if stock is insufficient, no payment is taken, so the system never ends up half-committed.

The subtle correctness concern I always raise is the race between adding to the cart and checking out, because an item can sell out in between. That is why the authoritative inventory check and decrement happen at checkout under a lock or an atomic operation, never when the item is first added, and why I keep all money in BigDecimal. In my banking work at National Bank of India, this is the same transactional discipline I apply to any purchase of a limited asset like gold coins, where the inventory check, payment, and stock deduction must succeed or fail together as one unit.
